from_notes: Centralized Bureaucracy: Highly centralized bureaucratic rule with the king at the pinnacle of power, exercising paternal despotism.
x: The Mauryan state was highly centralised and bureaucratic – a 'paternal despotism' with the king at the top of a large official hierarchy. Decentralised-feudal describes the post-Gupta age, not the Mauryas.

from_notes: Currency: Punch-marked silver coins with symbols like peacocks and hills formed the imperial currency of the Mauryas.
x: The Mauryas are credited with cultural patronage, division of the empire into provinces and an empire reaching the Hindukush. Their currency was punch-marked silver, so 'gold coins' is wrong and I, III and IV hold.

x: The five-sheath (pancha kosha) model comes from the Taittiriya Upanishad; in education it is elaborated in Sri Aurobindo's integral education (physical, vital, mental, psychic, spiritual), so the expected answer is Aurobindo.

from_notes: 7. Mitra: Allies

from_notes: The seven parts are: Swami, Amatya, Durga, Danda, Janapada, Kosha, Mitra
x: The Saptanga limbs are king, ministers, territory, fort, treasury, army and ally, so 'kings, territory, administration and treasury' is the only option drawn from them. The other options list unrelated groups.

from_notes: Samaharta: The Samaharta was the chief of the revenue department. He was the highest officer in charge of assessment and the collection of all revenue of the empire.
x: The Samaharta was the collector-general of revenue. The treasurer and keeper of stores was the Sannidhata, and agriculture was under the Sitadhyaksha.

from_notes: DANDA PALA: Chief Army officer
x: Among the 18 tirthas the Dandapala was the chief officer of the army. The treasury was under the Sannidhata and justice under the Pradeshtri and Vyavaharika.

from_notes: Samaharta (tax collector)
x: In the Arthashastra the Samaharta was the officer in charge of collecting revenue. The Sannidhata was the treasurer, the Sitadhyaksha the superintendent of crown land and the Samsthadhyaksha of markets.

x: In the 1921-22 no-tax campaign at Pedanandipadu (Guntur), led by Parvataneni Veeraiah Chowdary, village officers were made to resign so that no land revenue could be collected. The other options were not aims of the campaign.

evidence: AP History standard accounts of the Non-Cooperation Movement in Guntur (village officers resigned en masse)

x: In the medieval Deccan the Deshmukh was the hereditary revenue official of a pargana who collected land revenue from the peasants for the state. Chauth was a Maratha levy on territories, not the Deshmukh's duty.

from_notes: Pautavadhyaksha: Super-intendent of weight and measures.
x: The Pautavadhyaksha was the superintendent of weights and measures. The Sulkadhyaksha collected tolls, the Samsthadhyaksha supervised markets and the Panyadhyaksha commerce.

from_notes: Pautavadhyaksha: Super-intendent of weight and measures.
x: The Pautavadhyaksha was in charge of weights and measures. The Panyadhyaksha handled commerce, the Sitadhyaksha crown-land agriculture and the Sunadhyaksha the slaughterhouse.

from_notes: Sitadhyaksha: Super-intendent of crown land
x: Of the options, the Sitadhyaksha, superintendent of crown land, collected the land revenue (sita). The Shulkadhyaksha collected tolls and the Akaradhyaksha ran mines; the Samaharta, the chief revenue officer, is not offered.

from_notes: Sthaniya | 800; Dronamukha | 400; Kharvatika (Karvatika) | 200; Sangrahana | 10
x: The Arthashastra units are Sthaniya (800 villages), Dronamukha (400), Kharvatika (200) and Sangrahana (10), so only option C gives the hierarchy in order (largest to smallest). The question's 'ascending' means the order of the administrative ladder; no option gives it smallest-first.
source: APPSC Complete app notes (old-notes.txt) 37:4:4; Kautilya Arthashastra II.1

from_notes: Rajuka : Superintendent to look after Justice
x: Rajjukas were Mauryan officials named in Ashoka's edicts – district officers for land survey and assessment with judicial powers. They were not Chola traders, Gupta feudal lords or Saka soldiers.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 02 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-02.pdf) p.46; PMF2 p.114

from_notes: District administration: Pradesika, Rajuka and Yukta were officials at the district level.
x: Ashoka's inscriptions show the Pradeshika, Rajuka and Yukta as district-level officers (UPSC 2025 key B). The village level was under the Gramika and Gopa.

from_notes: District administration: Pradesika, Rajuka and Yukta were officials at the district level.
x: Yukta, Pradeshika and Rajjuka are all Mauryan officers named in Rock Edict III. Agraharika is not a Mauryan office.

from_notes: Rajukas managed districts.

from_notes: 3. Committee on Registration of Births and Deaths
x: Megasthenes' third municipal committee of Pataliputra registered births and deaths, a function municipalities still perform. Weights and prices were the fourth committee's work but are not the continuous municipal function asked.

from_notes: 3. Committee on Registration of Births and Deaths
x: Registration of births and deaths was the work of the third Mauryan city committee and remains municipal work today. Weights, prices and artisans do not show that continuity.

from_notes: Agronomoi = district officers (roads, irrigation, land measurement)
x: Megasthenes' Agronomoi were district officers who looked after roads, irrigation and land measurement, so 'construction of roads' is the field. Weights and measures belonged to the city committees.
source: APPSC Complete app notes (old-notes.txt) 37:6:0; Strabo XV.1.50 (Megasthenes fragment)

from_notes: Civic penalty: Pankodakasannirodhe – fine for slushing the road (dirt, water logging).
x: Pankodakasannirodhe was the Arthashastra fine for slushing the road with mud and water. It was not for filthy drinking water, garbage or temples.

from_notes: Sitadhyaksha: Super-intendent of crown land
x: Sita was the revenue from crown land, managed by the Sitadhyaksha. It is not a goddess, sect or barren land here.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 02 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-02.pdf) p.46; OLD 37:9:0.0

from_notes: Other Taxes: Included Pindakara (assessed on groups of villages)
x: The 'pin tax' is Pindakara, a tax assessed on groups of villages and paid by the village as a unit. Irrigation tax and labour dues were separate levies.

from_notes: Sales tax evasion: death (Megasthenes).
x: Megasthenes records that evasion of the sales tax was punished with death. Confiscation and imprisonment are not what he reports.

from_notes: Pranaya | Emergency tax ('gift of affection')
x: Pranaya was an emergency tax ('gift of affection') of the Arthashastra. It is not a marriage form, land grant or the regular land tax (bhaga).
source: APPSC Complete app notes (old-notes.txt) 37:9:0.4; NG2 p.50 (emergency taxes)

from_notes: Samaharta (tax collector)
x: The Samaharta handled revenue collection. The Vyavaharika was a civil judge, the Antapala guarded frontier forts and the Pradeshtha handled criminal justice.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 02 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-02.pdf) p.46; PMF2 p.113

from_notes: Mauryan kings did not bestow land grants on religious basis (land grants become common only from the Satavahanas)

from_notes: Pana (karshapana) | Silver (APPSC G2 2011)
x: The Mauryan silver coin was the Pana (karshapana); the Mashaka and Kakani were copper. Niska and Shatamana are older Vedic-era value units.

from_notes: Currency: Punch-marked silver coins with symbols like peacocks and hills formed the imperial currency of the Mauryas.
x: Mauryan coins were the silver punch-marked Pana with copper Mashaka and Kakani. Gold coinage began with the Indo-Greeks and Kushanas.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 02 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-02.pdf) p.46; PMF2 p.115

from_notes: Trading Centers: Tamralipti on the Eastern coast was a significant maritime trading center during the Mauryan era.
x: Tamralipti on the east coast was the main port of the Ganga basin in Mauryan times. Sopara and Bharukachchha were west-coast ports and Patala lay in the Indus delta.

from_notes: Slavery: Slavery could occur by birth, voluntary sale, capture in war, or judicial punishment, but Megasthenes did not find slaves in India.

from_notes: Divorce and remarriage allowed to a wife deserted by her husband
x: The Arthashastra allows a wife deserted by her husband to divorce (moksha) and remarry. The Manusmriti does not allow it.

from_notes: Divorce and remarriage allowed to a wife deserted by her husband
x: The Arthashastra permits divorce to a wife deserted by her husband or whose husband stays long abroad. The Kamasutra, Manusmriti and Sukranitisara do not.

from_notes: Seven classes: philosophers, farmers, herdsmen/hunters, artisans and traders, soldiers, overseers/spies, councillors and assessors.

from_notes: Introduction of burnt bricks and timber in construction, noted by Megasthenes in his writings about Pataliputra.

from_notes: Ashokan pillars at Rampurva, Lauriya Nandangarh, and Sarnath are circular and monolithic, made of Chunar sandstone.

from_notes: Ashokan pillars are free-standing, monolithic pillars
x: Ashokan pillars are free-standing monuments, not parts of buildings, so D is the incorrect statement. They are polished, monolithic and have tapering shafts.

from_notes: Ashokan pillars are free-standing, monolithic pillars
x: Ashokan stone pillars stand alone and are not parts of architectural structures. The other three statements (polished, monolithic, tapering) are true.

from_notes: They belonged to the Brahmin caste ... They were Hindus but also patronized Buddhism
x: The Satavahanas were Brahmanas who revived Vedic religion, so Hinduism (Brahmanism) was their religion; they also patronised Buddhism. Jainism was not their faith.

from_notes: Bhadrabahu's Kalpasutra, a significant literary work, is attributed to the Mauryan period.
x: The Kalpasutra of Bhadrabahu is a Jain canonical text on the lives of the Tirthankaras. The Vedic Kalpa Sutras share the name but the exam item means the Jain work.

from_notes: APPSC G1 2024: Dhauli elephant, Didarganj Yakshi, Sanchi stupa, Kumrahar hall – all four Mauryan.

from_notes: [UPSC CSE 2015] ... which one among the following was made earliest? Answer: b) Rock-cut Elephant at Dhauli

from_notes: [UPSC CSE 2015] ... Answer: b) Rock-cut Elephant at Dhauli
x: The Dhauli rock-cut elephant was carved under Ashoka in the 3rd c. BCE, earlier than the Udayagiri Varaha (5th c.), Mahabalipuram (7th–8th c.) and Lingaraja (10th–11th c.).

from_notes: Manibhadra Yaksha (inscribed) | Parkham (Mathura) – RPSC 2021

from_notes: Bharhut | Satna; Sunga, c. 150 BC; Dhamek | Sarnath; Ashokan original, Gupta present form

from_notes: Sanchi (Kaknam) | Raisen, MP

x: Stupas were linked to towns and trade routes, funded by merchants and guilds, and Ashoka popularised the cult. So 'located in rural areas' is the incorrect statement.

from_notes: The brick core of the Great Stupa was built in the time of Ashoka
x: Sanchi's Great Stupa was built by Ashoka (brick core); the Sungas cased it in stone. Chandragupta, Kautilya and the Buddha had no role.

from_notes: The brick core of the Great Stupa was built in the time of Ashoka
x: Ashoka built the original Sanchi Stupa. Pushyamitra's Sungas only enlarged it later; Bimbisara and Harsha are unrelated.

from_notes: Buddhist work 'Bhimasena Jataka' refers to Andhra Padha
x: The Bhimasena Jataka refers to Andhra Padha, marking out the Andhra region. The Serivanija Jataka names Andhapura and the Suttanipata the Bavari story.

from_notes: Chulla-Kalinga Jataka | Asmaka king Satakarni defeated Kharavela of Kalinga (APPSC G2 2008)
x: The Chulla-Kalinga Jataka tells of the Asmaka king defeating the king of Kalinga, which the APPSC key reads as Satakarni over Kharavela. Serivanija and Bhimasena Jatakas carry other Andhra references.

from_notes: Chulla-Kalinga Jataka | Asmaka king Satakarni defeated Kharavela of Kalinga (APPSC G2 2008)
x: The Chulla-Kalinga Jataka is the one cited for the Asmaka victory over Kalinga. The Rajavali-katha is a later Jain work.

from_notes: Assaka (Asmaka) | Bodhan (Podana) (APPSC G2 2012) | Godavari
x: Assaka's capital was Potali (Podana), modern Bodhan. Paithan (Pratishthana) was Mulaka's capital, and Dhanyakataka and Kotilingala are Satavahana centres.

from_notes: Megasthanese 'Indica' and 13th Major Rock Edict of Ashoka also mentioned about the people of Andhra
x: Megasthenes, Seleucus' ambassador, mentions the Andhras in his Indica. Pliny and Ptolemy wrote later and were not ambassadors; Marco Polo was a medieval traveller.

from_notes: Serivanija Jataka | Andhapura / Andhakapura – Andhra city reached across the river Telavaha by merchants
x: The Serivanija Jataka mentions Andhapura (Andhranagari), identified with Dhanyakataka. The Bhimasena Jataka gives Andhra Padha instead.

from_notes: Dhanyakataka: Buddhist centre of the Mahasanghikas; capital of the later Satavahanas
x: Dhanyakataka (Amaravati–Dharanikota) lies in Andhra on the Krishna and was a Mahasanghika centre (UPSC 2023). It is not in Gandhara, Kalinga or Magadha.

from_notes: Gottiprolu (Nellore region) | ASI dig: large settlement in a massive brick wall, 2nd–1st c. BCE; trade centre near an ancient seaport
x: The ASI's 2019 dig at Gottiprolu (Nellore) exposed an early-historic trade centre within a massive brick wall. Adurru is a Buddhist stupa site and Rajahmundry and Madakasira were not that dig.
Rea measured the Bhattiprolu stupa's dome at 132 ft across on a 148-ft base, the figure APPSC asks as its size. It is strictly a diameter, not a height; 133–135 ft are distractors.

dispute: Strictly 132 ft is the dome's diameter (base 148 ft, A. Rea); no source gives a 132-ft height.

from_notes: According to inscriptional evidence, the ruler of Bhattiprolu in 3rd century B.C. was Kubhiraka
x: The Bhattiprolu relic-casket inscriptions name Raja Kubhiraka (Kuberaka) as ruler of Bhattiprolu in the 3rd c. BCE.

from_notes: Eventually, the Satavahanas emerged as the mighty rulers of South India.
x: After the Mauryas the Satavahanas were the most powerful dynasty of the south. The Pallavas, Cholas and Chalukyas rose centuries later.

from_notes: Vasudeva Kanva founded the Kanva dynasty, which succeeded the Shungas.
x: The Kanvas, founded by Vasudeva Kanva after killing Devabhuti, followed the Sungas. The Satavahanas ended the Kanvas, and the Kushanas and Guptas came later.

from_notes: The last Mauryan king, Brihadratha ... was assassinated by his military commander, Pushyamitra Shunga
x: Brihadratha was killed by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Sunga. The other names are not tied to the coup.

from_notes: Ancestors of the Sungas came from Ujjain
x: Tradition places the Sungas' ancestral home at Ujjain, in Malwa. Magadha was their later seat of power.

from_notes: Last Mauryan → Brihadratha → assassinated by Pushyamitra Shunga → 185 BCE.
x: Brihadratha was the last Mauryan emperor. Jaloka was a legendary son of Ashoka in Kashmir, and Avantivarman and Nandivardhana are unrelated.
'The Stone that Speaketh' is the book of Durgabai Deshmukh, the freedom fighter and founder of the Andhra Mahila Sabha.
evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durgabai_Deshmukh

from_notes: Yavana invasion is in Gargi Samhita, Mahabhashya, Malavikagnimitram – NOT Visakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa
x: The Gargi Samhita, Patanjali's Mahabhashya and Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram record the Yavana invasions of the Sunga age. The Mudrarakshasa is about Chandragupta Maurya's rise.

from_notes: AYODHYA INSCRIPTION – Pushyamitra performed → 2 Ashvamedha Yajnas
x: The Ayodhya inscription of Dhanadeva records Pushyamitra's two Ashvamedhas. Besnagar is the Heliodorus pillar and Hathigumpha is Kharavela's.
source: Rocket Indian History 01 (src/indian-history/rocket-indian-history-01.pdf) p.7; PMF Art & Culture 04 p.29

from_notes: AYODHYA INSCRIPTION – Pushyamitra performed → 2 Ashvamedha Yajnas
x: The Ayodhya inscription records the two Ashvamedhas of Pushyamitra. Sarnath, Besnagar and Hathigumpha are unrelated.

Skandagupta's Bhitari pillar records victories over the Pushyamitras (read here as 'Sungas') and the Hunas, and Vakataka pressure is also linked to his reign; no Kalinga conquest is recorded. So the Kalingas is the expected answer.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-03.pdf) p.64 (Bhitari: Pushyamitras and Hunas)
evidence: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-03.pdf) p.64

from_notes: Malavikagnimitra ... provides information about the Shunga dynasty, particularly the founder, Pushyamitra Sunga, and his son, Agnimitra.
x: Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram is the love story of Agnimitra, son of the Sunga founder Pushyamitra. Swapnavasavadatta is Bhasa's and Ratnavali Harsha's.

from_notes: Malavikagnimitram: Kalidasa's first play, 5 acts; love story of Agnimitra and Malavika.
x: Agnimitra, Pushyamitra's son, is the hero of Malavikagnimitram. Pushyamitra appears only as the reigning king.

from_notes: Malavikagnimitra ... Pushyamitra Sunga, and his son, Agnimitra.
x: Malavikagnimitram tells of Agnimitra, son of Pushyamitra, and Malavika. The other works are about other heroes.

from_notes: Patanjali, the author of Mahabhashya, was a contemporary of Pushyamitra Shunga.
x: Patanjali, author of the Mahabhashya, was a contemporary of Pushyamitra Sunga. He was not linked to either Chandragupta or to Ashoka.

from_notes: Besnagar (Bhilsa/Vidisha), MP ... Garuda-dhvaja dedicated to Vasudeva
x: The Besnagar Garudadhvaja is a 2nd c. BCE Sunga-period monument, so it is not Gupta. The Sarnath Buddhas, the Deogarh temple and the Nalanda copper Buddha are Gupta-period works.

from_notes: FIRST: earliest inscriptional proof of Bhagavatism
x: The Besnagar inscription of Heliodorus is the earliest inscriptional evidence of the Bhagavata religion. The Allahabad, Bhitari and Mehrauli inscriptions are Gupta-period.

from_notes: Garuda-dhvaja dedicated to Vasudeva (Vishnu)
x: Heliodorus set up the Garudadhvaja in honour of Vasudeva, 'god of gods', alone. Sankarshana and Pradyumna are not named on it.

from_notes: Bharhut ... 'fine example of Shunga architecture' (RPSC 2023)
x: The Bharhut stupa railings and gateways (c. 150 BCE) are a fine example of Sunga art. It is not Kushana, Gupta or Chola.

from_notes: Buddhist texts like the Divyavadana accuse them of persecuting Buddhists and damaging monasteries.
x: Pushyamitra Sunga, a patron of Brahmanical sacrifices, did not spread Buddhism; Buddhist texts even call him a persecutor. Ashoka, Kanishka and Harsha were great patrons of Buddhism.

from_notes: Sanchi gateway: Ashoka visits the Bodhi tree with two queens.
x: The Sanchi gateway shows Ashoka's visit to the Bodhi tree with his two queens. Bharhut, Sonari and Satdhara do not have this relief.

from_notes: Devabhuti, the last Shunga king, was murdered by his minister Vasudeva Kanva ...
x: All three are correct: Pushyamitra killed Brihadratha, Vasudeva Kanva killed Devabhuti, and the last Kanva Susharman was deposed by the Andhras (Satavahanas).
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-03.pdf) p.5, p.25; R1 p.95
